Choosing an Air Temperature Forecast Source

Source: vignettes/air-temperature-source.Rmd
air-temperature-source.Rmd

Every RM 8.5 water-temperature model in this project is driven by a forecast of air temperature over the next one to seven days. Which archive supplies that forecast turns out to matter less than most people expect — but how that archive is structured matters a great deal, and one of the options has a defect that silently removes the entire forecast signal.

This vignette records what we checked, what we found, and what to use. The first section runs live against the package’s own data so you can confirm the central claim yourself; the later sections report measurements made against external archives and cite the scripts that produced them.

library(whychusModel)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)

1. The shipped archive carries no lead-specific information

all_historical_forecasts looks like a proper forecast archive. It has a valid_date (the day being forecast), an issue_date (the day the forecast was made), and lead_days running 1 through 7. Naively you would build a seven-day trajectory from it and expect seven different numbers.

Start by looking at how it is laid out:

all_historical_forecasts |>
  mutate(valid_date = as.Date(valid_date)) |>
  group_by(lead_days, type) |>
  summarise(n = n(), first = min(valid_date), last = max(valid_date),
            .groups = "drop")
#> # A tibble: 8 × 5
#>   lead_days type                    n first      last      
#>       <dbl> <chr>               <int> <date>     <date>    
#> 1         0 historical weather   8766 2011-01-01 2018-12-31
#> 2         1 historical forecast  8319 2019-01-01 2026-08-04
#> 3         2 historical forecast  8319 2019-01-01 2026-08-04
#> 4         3 historical forecast  8319 2019-01-01 2026-08-04
#> 5         4 historical forecast  8319 2019-01-01 2026-08-04
#> 6         5 historical forecast  8319 2019-01-01 2026-08-04
#> 7         6 historical forecast  8319 2019-01-01 2026-08-04
#> 8         7 historical forecast  8319 2019-01-01 2026-08-04

Two things are already visible. lead_days == 0 is ERA5 reanalysis (“historical weather”) covering 2011–2018, and leads 1–7 are the “historical forecast” covering 2019 onward. They do not overlap — this is not an observed series running alongside a forecast series, it is two different products spliced end to end. Any analysis that treats lead 0 as “the truth” against which leads 1–7 can be scored will silently join zero rows.

Now the important part. Group by issue_date and count how many distinct values that issue date carries across its seven leads:

by_issue <- all_historical_forecasts |>
  filter(variable == "temperature_2m_max", !is.na(issue_date), lead_days %in% 1:7) |>
  group_by(issue_date) |>
  summarise(n_leads = n(), n_distinct_values = n_distinct(value), .groups = "drop")

table(by_issue$n_distinct_values)
#> 
#>    1 
#> 2779

Every issue date carries exactly one distinct value across all seven leads. Laid out for a single issue date it is unmistakable:

all_historical_forecasts |>
  filter(variable == "temperature_2m_max",
         issue_date == as.Date("2024-07-10"), lead_days %in% 1:7) |>
  transmute(issue_date, lead_days, valid_date = as.Date(valid_date), value) |>
  arrange(lead_days)
#> # A tibble: 7 × 4
#>   issue_date lead_days valid_date value
#>   <date>         <dbl> <date>     <dbl>
#> 1 2024-07-10         1 2024-07-11  40.7
#> 2 2024-07-10         2 2024-07-12  40.7
#> 3 2024-07-10         3 2024-07-13  40.7
#> 4 2024-07-10         4 2024-07-14  40.7
#> 5 2024-07-10         5 2024-07-15  40.7
#> 6 2024-07-10         6 2024-07-16  40.7
#> 7 2024-07-10         7 2024-07-17  40.7

One number, stamped onto the next seven days.

Why this is easy to miss

Slice the data the other way — fix the valid date and vary the lead — and the values differ, which looks reassuringly like real forecast behaviour:

all_historical_forecasts |>
  filter(variable == "temperature_2m_max",
         valid_date == as.Date("2024-07-16"), lead_days %in% 1:7) |>
  transmute(lead_days, issue_date, valid_date = as.Date(valid_date), value) |>
  arrange(lead_days)
#> # A tibble: 7 × 4
#>   lead_days issue_date valid_date value
#>       <dbl> <date>     <date>     <dbl>
#> 1         1 2024-07-15 2024-07-16  33.4
#> 2         2 2024-07-14 2024-07-16  36.3
#> 3         3 2024-07-13 2024-07-16  37.5
#> 4         4 2024-07-12 2024-07-16  35.8
#> 5         5 2024-07-11 2024-07-16  35.2
#> 6         6 2024-07-10 2024-07-16  40.7
#> 7         7 2024-07-09 2024-07-16  40.3

They differ only because you are reading seven different issue dates down that column. The variation is between issue dates, not across leads. It is worth being precise about this, because “the values differ by lead” is true for this slice and false in the way that matters.

The consequence for feature building

Feature code in this project builds a trajectory for a run date R by taking air_max_dk from the row with lead_days == k and valid_date == R + k. That row’s issue date is R + k - k = R — so every column in the trajectory comes from the same issue date, and therefore carries the same value:

get_lead <- function(k) {
  all_historical_forecasts |>
    filter(lead_days == k, variable == "temperature_2m_max") |>
    transmute(run_date = as.Date(valid_date) - k, "d{k}" := value)
}

traj <- Reduce(function(a, b) full_join(a, b, by = "run_date"),
               lapply(1:7, get_lead)) |>
  tidyr::drop_na()

spread <- apply(as.matrix(traj[, paste0("d", 1:7)]), 1, function(r) max(r) - min(r))

c(run_dates = nrow(traj),
  pct_all_seven_identical = round(mean(spread == 0) * 100, 1),
  mean_spread_C = round(mean(spread), 4))
#>               run_dates pct_all_seven_identical           mean_spread_C 
#>                    2767                     100                       0
head(traj, 4)
#> # A tibble: 4 × 8
#>   run_date      d1    d2    d3    d4    d5    d6    d7
#>   <date>     <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1 2018-12-31   1     1     1     1     1     1     1  
#> 2 2019-01-01   1.4   1.4   1.4   1.4   1.4   1.4   1.4
#> 3 2019-01-02   2.4   2.4   2.4   2.4   2.4   2.4   2.4
#> 4 2019-01-03   9.7   9.7   9.7   9.7   9.7   9.7   9.7

The entire seven-day air-temperature trajectory collapses to a single repeated number, on 100% of run dates. A model built on this does not see a forecast at all — it sees today’s conditions replicated forward, and whatever skill it shows at long leads comes from persistence and seasonal timing rather than from any knowledge of the coming week.

This is the defect that motivated moving to an external source. It does not make all_historical_forecasts useless — it is a long, consistent record and remains the only source here reaching back to 2011 — but it should be understood as a best-estimate weather series indexed by issue date, not as a per-lead forecast archive.

2. dynamical.org GFS: genuine leads, one aggregation trap

dynamical.org publishes NOAA GFS output as Icechunk/Zarr on S3. Its forecasts genuinely vary by lead, and data-raw/pull_dynamical_forecasts.py retrieves them.

One trap is worth knowing about, because getting it wrong produces plausible-looking numbers. Per the dataset’s own variable metadata, maximum_temperature_2m and minimum_temperature_2m are each “Maximum / Minimum over the previous 1–6 hours, reset every 6-hour forecast step” — they are not calendar-day aggregates. Selecting the single step that lands on a target day’s 00Z captures only the last six hours before midnight, which misses the afternoon peak and the pre-dawn low entirely:

Aggregation Daily max bias Daily min bias
Naive single-step −2.7 °C +8.0 °C
Four 6-hour steps, reduced correctly −2.1 °C −0.2 °C

The pull script reconstructs each calendar day from the four non-overlapping six-hour windows that tile it (max of the maxima, min of the minima, mean of the cloud means). Two smaller gotchas it also handles: GFS initialises every six hours, so an unfiltered pull returns four runs per day (it keeps 00Z by default); and .sel(method = "nearest") has no bounds checking, so a request predating coverage silently snaps onto the earliest available date rather than being dropped.

Coverage begins 2021-05-01.

3. Match the product you actually serve

The operational forecast is driven by the NWS gridded product from weather.gov, logged daily to output/nws-forecasts-log.csv. Training on GFS while serving NWS is a train/serve mismatch, and it is measurable. Comparing each candidate archive against the NWS forecasts actually issued for the same run date and lead in 2026 (n = 588):

Max air temperature Bias MAE r
Open-Meteo Previous Runs +0.03 °C 1.58 °C 0.949
dynamical.org GFS −0.47 °C 2.03 °C 0.913

MAE against NWS grows with lead for both — from about 1.1 °C at lead 1 to 2.3 °C at lead 7 for Open-Meteo, and 1.7 to 2.8 °C for dynamical.org.

Cloud cover is poorly matched in every source tested (+13 to +15 percentage points versus NWS, r 0.76–0.80), so it is not a discriminator between them.

The ideal training set would be an archive of NDFD, the exact product weather.gov serves. It is not practically obtainable: the AWS open-data bucket (noaa-ndfd-pds) is a rolling live mirror whose files are overwritten in place with no date partitioning, and NCEI’s deep archive is served through a request system limited to one day of data per request.

4. Open-Meteo Previous Runs: better inputs, no better forecasts

Open-Meteo’s Previous Runs API (previous-runs-api.open-meteo.com, retrieved by data-raw/pull_openmeteo_previous_runs.py) is a genuine per-lead archive — only ~2% of days show identical lead-1 and lead-7 values, and error decays the way real forecast skill does (MAE 0.91 °C at lead 1 to 2.64 °C at lead 7).

Given it also matches NWS better, it ought to produce better water temperature forecasts. It does not. Retraining the identical model on each source and scoring both on the real 2026 hindcast (paired t-test on squared error, n = 357):

Contrast (only the source differs) ΔRMSE p
Absolute target: Open-Meteo vs dynamical +0.072 < 0.001 (dynamical better)
Delta target: Open-Meteo vs dynamical −0.038 0.015 (Open-Meteo better)
Best configuration: Open-Meteo vs dynamical −0.010 0.46 — not significant

The source even changes sign depending on model framing, and at the configuration actually in use the two are statistically indistinguishable. For comparison, changing the model’s target from absolute temperature to change-from-today is worth −0.29 to −0.40 RMSE (p < 0.001) — six to ten times larger than anything the source choice buys.

A 0.45 °C improvement in input quality buys nothing because the model is anchored on RM 8.5’s own observed temperature, not on the air-temperature forecast. That anchor dominates.

One practical caveat: this archive’s cloud_cover_previous_dayN only begins 2024-04-15, while temperature reaches back to 2021. A cloud-using model is therefore limited to about two and a half seasons from this source — though cloud measured as irrelevant under the change-from-today framing (p = 0.88), so that is rarely binding.

5. Verdict

Use dynamical.org GFS (data-raw/dynamical_gfs_air_temp_historical.csv). Not because it is the best match to NWS — it isn’t — but because the source choice does not measurably affect forecast skill, and it is already integrated with cloud cover back to 2021.

  • Do not build lead-varying features from all_historical_forecasts. Use it for its long record, its seasonal climatology, or as a best-estimate weather series — not as a forecast trajectory.
  • Open-Meteo Previous Runs is a fine alternative and a reasonable swap if pipeline simplicity matters: it pulls in seconds against dynamical’s twenty-plus minutes of Zarr point extraction, and needs only requests rather than icechunk/xarray/zarr/s3fs.
  • Spend effort elsewhere. Target framing, and eventually training on the accumulating output/nws-forecasts-log.csv once it spans two or three seasons, both matter far more. That log is unreproducible if lost and worth protecting.

Pulling each source 

# dynamical.org GFS (default: leads 1-7, RM 8.5, writes to data-raw/)
#   python data-raw/pull_dynamical_forecasts.py
#
# Open-Meteo Previous Runs
#   python data-raw/pull_openmeteo_previous_runs.py --start-year 2021 --end-year 2026

Both write a long-format CSV with the same schema — init_date, valid_date, lead_days, variable, value, with variable in temperature_2m_max, temperature_2m_min, cloud_cover_mean — so they are drop-in comparable.

Measurements in sections 2–4 come from data-raw/dynamical-vs-openmeteo-comparison.Rmd and the source comparison in analysis/rm85-rf-delta.Rmd; they are reported here rather than recomputed because they depend on files under data-raw/ and output/, which are not installed with the package.
